messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame Mensah, a 55-year-old bomb disposal technician, came to treatment after months of insisting to himself that he should be able to handle this on his own. He was a married man who had spent years working in high-risk situations with a professional calm that others admired. What unsettled him most now was that the event that had broken through that calm had not happened on the job at all, but during a natural disaster, in circumstances where there had been nothing to assess, contain, or control.

The disaster had unfolded fast. During a severe storm, the neighborhood where Kwame and his wife lived was thrown into chaos by violent winds, structural damage, and sudden blasts of noise from objects tearing loose and crashing. What stayed with him were not neat, continuous memories but fragments: a deafening bang nearby, people shouting over one another, the sense that the situation was changing by the second and no one knew what would happen next. He remembered the atmosphere of total unpredictability more than a coherent sequence of events. That loss of order was especially jarring for a man whose work depended on procedure and controlled response. When he tried to describe the worst moments, he often stopped short, as if his mind shut a door before he could get all the way there. He would begin with one image or sound, then go silent, jaw tight, saying only that there were pieces missing. The parts that did come back were charged with intense anger. He found himself suddenly furious when he remembered the shouting, the confusion, the sense of being trapped inside a situation where skill and training meant nothing.

In the weeks afterward, his reactions did not settle in the way he expected. Loud noises became difficult immediately. A slammed car door, a metal tray dropped in a kitchen, raised voices from across a parking lot could make his whole body jolt before he had time to tell himself what it was. He described this with embarrassment and frustration: his body moved first, heart pounding, muscles tensed, before his mind had caught up. Sometimes, for a few seconds, he felt as though he were back inside the storm’s chaos rather than in the present. Those moments frightened him because they arrived so abruptly. He knew, once they passed, that nothing was actually wrong, yet in the moment he reacted as if danger were right there.

At work, this became especially troubling. As a bomb disposal technician, he was accustomed to taking loud sounds and urgent situations seriously, but now unpredictability itself felt intolerable. If a colleague shouted across the worksite without warning, Kwame’s entire body surged into alarm. If a situation developed in a way that was not clearly structured, he felt a rising need to get away from it. He began quietly arranging his days to minimize exposure to anything that might feel stressful. He volunteered less for situations he could not map out in advance, lingered in controlled spaces, and avoided unnecessary conversations if he thought they might become heated. He did not explain much. He told himself he was being practical, but over time it narrowed both his work life and home life.

At home, his wife saw that he was never really at rest. If he was not working, he kept his mind occupied constantly with television, his phone, chores, or background noise, as though stillness might leave too much room for memory. He ate more than he wanted to, often in the evening, describing it as the only thing that seemed to settle him for a while. He avoided stressful errands, difficult family discussions, crowded or noisy settings, anything that might bring shouting or sudden commotion. These habits accumulated quietly. His wife experienced him as present in the room but hard to reach, distracted or irritable, always steering life toward what felt manageable and away from what did not.

What finally brought Kwame in was not one dramatic collapse but the growing recognition that he was organizing his life around the possibility of being caught off guard. Recently, after hearing loud voices and a sudden crash in a public place, he reacted before he could think, and for a moment he was no longer there at all but inside the disaster again. He was shaken not only by the intensity of the reaction but by how little warning he had had. He said he could not trust his own mind to give him the full memory, only pieces, and he could not trust his body not to respond as if the danger were happening again. He came to treatment wanting relief, but also wanting to understand why a man who had built his life around managing threat now felt so defenseless in the face of noise, shouting, and the simple fact that something unexpected might happen. What frightened him most was the sense that the next false alarm could come anywhere, at work or at home, and that he would again be overtaken before he even knew what he was reacting to.
